Synchrotron X-ray radio-topography was used to characterize the growth and deformation of dendrites in the nickel-based superalloy CMSX-4.
Both permanent and transient deformation modes were observed, including localized deformation from gravity loading and reversible deformation from thermal contraction.
Diffraction contrast imaging revealed that the dendrite backbone is flexible, with only portions of the dendrite meeting the diffraction condition at a given time.

Digital image correlation analysis showed that the lateral contraction of the dendrite array due to cooling in the temperature gradient led to the generation of small misorientations between primary dendrites.
The primary dendrite arm spacing decreased from 130 to 124 μm during the course of the experiment due to thermal contraction.
The deformation of the dendrites was observed to affect their growth kinetics, with the reoriented dendrite able to competitively overgrow adjacent dendrites.
The study provides direct evidence of the transient phenomena that can lead to the formation of casting defects such as low- to medium-angle grain boundaries.
A temperature gradient of approximately 40 K/cm was imposed across the samples during directional solidification.
The diffraction topograph showed pristine dendrites with small misorientations between different portions of the same dendrite.
The diffraction contrast radiographs revealed that the deformation of the dendrites was reversible, with the extinction spot moving up and down the dendrite backbone.
The digital image correlation analysis indicated that the deformation was localized, with 'hot spots' of increased bending occurring where secondary dendrite arms impinged on each other.

The study concludes that the deformation of dendrites during solidification, particularly from thermal contraction, may be a key factor in the formation of small misorientations observed in single crystal castings.
The experimental setup used a bespoke Bridgman furnace designed for high-temperature solidification imaging experiments.
Radiographic images were captured using an ESRF Fast Readout Low Noise (FReLoN) CCD camera with a pixel size of 7.46 μm at a rate of 0.2 Hz.
Diffraction topographs were captured on photographic film (Agfa Structurix D3-SC, 17.6 x 12.5 cm2).
